readerTitle: The hire that would have sunk a growing studio
caseNote: 가상 사례 (디자인 스튜디오, B2B SaaS) + Paul Graham의 2015년 에세이 'Default Alive or Default Dead?'의 개념 · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 생존 여부는 성장 속도나 남은 현금 하나로 보지 않는다. 지금의 비용과 성장 속도로 현금이 바닥나기 전에 흑자에 닿는지를 함께 계산해야 보인다.
misconception: 매출이 빠르게 늘고 사람을 더 뽑을 만큼 일이 밀려 있으면 사업은 안전하다. 성장에 투자하면 생존 가능성도 높아진다.

sources.text: Graham, P. (2015). Default Alive or Default Dead? paulgraham.com
스튜디오와 SaaS 수치는 모두 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 채용 후 계산: 비용 $140k/월, 매출 매월 +$5k. 월 손실 50, 45, 40, 35, 30 → 5개월 누적 $200k로 현금 소진. 매출이 비용을 따라잡는 시점은 10개월 뒤(11개월째 $140k). 같은 기간 손실 합계는 $275k.
SaaS 계산: 현금 $600k, 매출 $20k/월이 매월 10% 성장, 비용 $100k/월 고정. 20×1.1^n = 100 → n ≈ 16.9개월(약 17개월). 누적 손실은 8개월에 약 $571k, 9개월에 약 $628k라서 현금은 약 8개월 버팀.
Graham이 에세이에서 '자신이 만나는 창업자 중 상당수(원문에서는 약 절반)가 이 답을 모른다'고 쓴 부분은 게시 전에 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 'many founders'로만 적었습니다.

cards.title: The hire that would have sunk a growing studio
body: Maya runs a small design studio. Revenue has grown every month this year, and clients are waiting in line.
To keep up, she plans to hire two more designers. It looks like the obvious move for a business that's doing well. The numbers say it would have closed the studio in five months.

image.label: A busy design studio with a calendar running out
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 디자인 스튜디오 책상 위에 상승하는 매출 그래프 포스터가 붙어 있고, 옆 벽 달력은 다섯 장만 남아 마지막 장이 흐릿하게 사라지는 연출. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Will Maya's studio make it?
body: The studio has $200k in the bank. It earns $90k a month and spends $120k. Revenue has been rising by about $3k each month.
Which question tells you the most about whether the studio survives?

options.feedback: Growth matters, but on its own it says nothing about whether the money lasts long enough for that growth to pay off.

options.text: How many months of cash are left?
options.feedback: A useful number, but it assumes losses stay the same. Here they shrink every month as revenue grows.

options.text: Will revenue catch up with costs before the cash runs out?
options.feedback: This combines both numbers into one answer: yes or no. It's the question this lesson is built on.

cards.title: On her current path, Maya makes it.
body: Each month the loss shrinks by $3k as revenue climbs. After about 10 months, revenue matches costs, with **$35k** still in the bank.

cards.title: Growing faster, dying sooner.
body: Two designers add $20k a month in costs. With more hands, revenue grows faster: $5k a month instead of $3k.
But the first month's loss jumps to $50k, then $45k, $40k. By month five, the $200k is gone. Revenue would only have caught up in month ten.
The plan that looked like success turns a business that survives into one that runs out of cash.

image.label: Two paths: cash line hitting zero before break-even
image.brief: 두 개의 선 그래프 비교. 왼쪽 "Today": 현금 선이 내려가다가 10개월째 $35k에서 멈추고 매출 선이 비용 선과 만남. 오른쪽 "With two hires": 현금 선이 5개월째 0에 닿고, 매출과 비용이 만나는 점(10개월)은 점선으로 멀리 표시.

cards.title: Default alive or default dead
body: Investor Paul Graham put it as one question in a 2015 essay. If your costs stay where they are and revenue keeps growing at its recent pace, do you reach profit before the money runs out?
If yes, you're **default alive**. If no, you're **default dead**: something has to change, or the business ends.
Graham noted that many founders he talked to didn't know which one they were.

cards.title: Default dead is a warning, not a verdict.
body: Being default dead doesn't mean you will fail. It means survival depends on something that hasn't happened yet: new money, lower costs or faster growth.
The danger is assuming that rescue will come. Founders often plan on raising money or landing a big client, then discover too late that it takes months or never arrives.
Knowing early gives you time to choose. A restaurant opening a second site or a builder buying new equipment faces the same test.

cards.title: The answer is only as good as your growth guess.
body: The test assumes recent growth continues. In a services business, one big client leaving can erase months of growth overnight. Test a slower path too.
Default dead can also be a deliberate bet, if funding is already committed and not just hoped for.
And cutting everything to look alive can stop the growth that was carrying you to break-even.

cards.title: Now it's a software startup.
body: Your subscription software has $600k in the bank. Revenue is $20k a month and growing 10% monthly. Costs are $100k a month.
At this pace, revenue catches costs in about 17 months. Your cash lasts about 8. What do you do?

options.text: Keep hiring. Strong growth will make raising money easy
options.feedback: You gain speed but bet the company on a round that isn't promised. If investors hesitate, you have no time left to adjust.

options.text: Start raising now, and prepare cuts that make you default alive if no deal closes by month four
options.feedback: You keep growing while the door is open and still control your fate if it closes. The cost is real effort spent planning cuts you may never use.

options.text: Freeze all spending tonight, including marketing
options.feedback: Losses drop fast, but the 10% growth may drop with them. You could end up alive but stuck, with nothing left to raise money on.

cards.title: Know whether you survive without help.
body: Growth and cash in the bank don't answer the question on their own. Put them together: on today's path, does revenue catch costs before the money runs out?
**Try it today:** write down your cash, monthly costs, monthly revenue and recent growth. Count the months to break-even and the months until cash runs out. Which comes first?
